passage:
Sound travels faster in warmer water and faster under greater pressure. In the open ocean these two influences work against each other. Near the surface, temperature falls steeply with depth, so sound slows as it descends. Below about a kilometre the temperature is already close to freezing and changes little, while pressure keeps rising, so sound speeds up again. Between the two lies a depth at which sound moves more slowly than at any depth above or below it.

A sound wave that strays upward out of this layer enters faster water and is bent back down; one that strays below it is bent back up. The layer therefore behaves as a waveguide, and a modest signal released inside it can be detected thousands of kilometres away. Oceanographers call it the deep sound channel. Its depth is not fixed. In polar water, where the surface is already cold, the channel rises almost to the surface.
prompt: [Academic — Oceanography] What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Long-range detection of sound at sea is possible only where the surface water is already cold.
Two opposing influences on sound speed create a depth that traps sound and carries it far.
Measurements of ocean temperature are more reliable below one kilometre than they are near the surface.
Sound in seawater travels faster than sound in air, and the gap widens with depth.
correct_answer: Two opposing influences on sound speed create a depth that traps sound and carries it far.
explanation: The passage opens with the opposed effects of temperature and pressure, derives a slow layer between them, and ends with signals detected thousands of kilometres away; that is the option about two opposing influences producing a trapping depth. The air-comparison option introduces a contrast the passage never draws; the temperature-measurement option makes a claim about instruments, not sound; and the polar option turns a remark about where the channel sits into a condition on whether it works at all.

choices: the channel would form deeper down, though it would still carry sound over long distances.

sound would travel faster at every depth than it now does.

correct_answer: no deep sound channel would form there.
explanation: The channel exists because the slowing effect of falling temperature stops and the speeding effect of pressure takes over; if temperature kept falling steeply there would be no turning point and so nothing to trap the sound. The option that keeps the channel but moves it deeper assumes the turning point survives, which is exactly what the premise removes. Nothing in the passage makes sound faster everywhere, and pressure's effect is physical, not altered by what temperature does.

passage:
The deep sea floor was long pictured as a place of near-perfect stillness, where particles settling from above accumulate undisturbed at a rate of a few millimetres per thousand years. Photographs taken in the 1970s beneath the Gulf Stream showed something else: ripples in the sediment, scoured hollows around stones, and, on one occasion, water so clouded that the camera recorded nothing.

The events responsible are now called benthic storms. They are driven not by weather at the surface but by eddies that break away from strong surface currents and sink, carrying energy downward over weeks. A storm may last ten days and move more sediment than the preceding decade of quiet settling.

For sediment cores, which are read as a record of past climate, the consequence is awkward. A core is assumed to lay down its layers in order. Where storms have passed, older material can be redeposited above younger.
prompt: [Academic — Oceanography] According to the passage, benthic storms are set in motion by
choices: eddies that break away from surface currents and sink.
the movement of stones across the sea floor.
the slow settling of particles from the surface.
weather systems passing over the Gulf Stream at the surface.
correct_answer: eddies that break away from surface currents and sink.
explanation: The passage states the driver directly and rules out surface weather in the same sentence, which disposes of the surface-weather option. Settling particles are the quiet background the storms interrupt, and the stones appear only as objects that scoured hollows form around.

passage:
A page of early printed text required, before anything could be printed at all, a sequence of three objects. The punchcutter filed the letter in relief on the end of a steel rod; this punch was driven into a bar of soft copper to sink an intaglio image, the matrix; molten lead alloy poured into a mould held against the matrix produced the type itself. Only the third was made in quantity.

The order of the work explains an oddity in the record. Punches survive in numbers; matrices are rarer; loose type from the fifteenth century is almost unknown. Type was consumable. It wore, and worn type was melted and recast, often as a different face. A printer who owned a set of punches owned the means of making type indefinitely, and punches were accordingly inventoried, bequeathed, and sometimes seized for debt. Historians who wish to trace a printing house therefore follow its punches rather than its books.
prompt: [Academic — History] Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
choices: Printing houses kept careful inventories because their creditors required them to.
The quality of early printing depended chiefly on the skill of the punchcutter.
Type was made in three stages, and the earlier tools outlasted the type.
Fifteenth-century printers preferred copper to lead because copper wore more slowly.
correct_answer: Type was made in three stages, and the earlier tools outlasted the type.
explanation: The passage sets out punch, matrix and type, then explains that punches survive in numbers while loose type is almost unknown; the option pairing the three stages with the survival of the earlier tools covers both halves. Punchcutting skill is never linked to print quality; copper and lead are used at different stages rather than compared for wear; and inventories are mentioned as evidence of value, not as a creditor's requirement.

passage:
Early printers proofread while the press ran. When an error was noticed the press was stopped, the offending type corrected, and printing resumed; the sheets already pulled were not thrown away, because paper was the largest single cost of the book. A finished edition therefore contained copies in both states, bound indifferently.

This is why no two copies of some early books are quite alike, and why the phrase 'the first edition' can mislead. Bibliographers compare surviving copies page by page to establish which state came first, using evidence such as a correction that introduces a new error of its own.

The habit also frustrates a natural assumption. A reader who finds a clean text may hold a late-state copy of a badly set book, while a reader who finds errors may hold the earlier one. Neither copy tells its own story; the story is in the comparison.

correct_answer: bound into finished copies alongside the corrected sheets.
explanation: The passage says the sheets already pulled were not thrown away and that a finished edition contained copies in both states, bound indifferently, which is the option about binding them alongside the corrected sheets. That directly contradicts the destruction option, and neither a reduced price nor a deliberate record is mentioned.

passage:
Leafcutter ants do not eat the leaves they carry. The fragments are chewed to a pulp and fed to a fungus that the colony cultivates in underground chambers; the ants eat the fungus. The arrangement is old enough that neither partner is now found without the other.

A monoculture of one fungus, kept in a warm, humid chamber, is an obvious target for parasites, and one mould in particular, Escovopsis, specialises in attacking it. The colony's defence is a third organism. Bacteria of the genus Pseudonocardia grow in pits in the ants' cuticle, nourished by glandular secretions, and produce compounds that suppress the mould.

The relationship is not simply cooperative. Escovopsis strains isolated from older colonies show reduced sensitivity to the bacterial compounds, and the bacteria carried by those colonies differ correspondingly. What looks like a settled partnership is better read as a standoff held in place by continual change on both sides.

correct_answer: chewed to a pulp and fed to a fungus the colony cultivates.
explanation: The first two sentences say the ants do not eat the leaves and that the pulp goes to the fungus, which rules out the option that has the ants eat them. Lining chambers and storing the fragments are uses the passage never assigns to the leaves.

passage:
Leafcutter ants do not eat the leaves they carry. The fragments are chewed to a pulp and fed to a fungus that the colony cultivates in underground chambers; the ants eat the fungus. The arrangement is old enough that neither partner is now found without the other.

A monoculture of one fungus, kept in a warm, humid chamber, is an obvious target for parasites, and one mould in particular, Escovopsis, specialises in attacking it. The colony's defence is a third organism. Bacteria of the genus Pseudonocardia grow in pits in the ants' cuticle, nourished by glandular secretions, and produce compounds that suppress the mould.

The relationship is not simply cooperative. Escovopsis strains isolated from older colonies show reduced sensitivity to the bacterial compounds, and the bacteria carried by those colonies differ correspondingly. What looks like a settled partnership is better read as a standoff held in place by continual change on both sides.
prompt: [Academic — Biology] The observation that Escovopsis from older colonies resists the bacterial compounds most supports which conclusion?

The ants acquire their bacteria from the fungus garden rather than from one another.
The parasite and the bacteria are still changing in response to each other.
correct_answer: The parasite and the bacteria are still changing in response to each other.
explanation: The resistance finding is paired with a matching difference in the bacteria those colonies carry, and a change on each side answering the other is what the passage calls a standoff held in place by continual change. Losing the garden is an outcome the passage never reports; the bacteria of older colonies differ rather than fail, so the option about declining usefulness reads only half the evidence; and where the ants get their bacteria is not discussed.

passage:
Many aphids excrete honeydew, a sugary waste of the phloem sap they feed on, and many ants collect it. Ants that tend a colony of aphids also drive off ladybirds and parasitic wasps, and the arrangement is usually described as mutual benefit.

Measurement complicates the description. Tended aphids grow more slowly and produce fewer offspring than untended aphids of the same species kept from predators by a mesh cage. Ants also remove individuals from the colony and eat them, most often when the honeydew yield per aphid falls.

The benefit to the aphid, then, is not an increase in its own output but a reduction in the variance of its fate: without ants a colony can be destroyed in a day, and with them it is cropped steadily. Whether that trade is worth making depends on how many predators are about, which differs from meadow to meadow.

correct_answer: each aphid is yielding less honeydew.
explanation: The passage attaches the eating directly to a fall in honeydew yield per aphid. Predator numbers govern whether the arrangement is worth it to the aphids rather than when ants eat them; colony size is never given as a trigger; and richer sap would raise yield, which is the opposite condition.

passage:
Before 1841 a screw and its nut were made as a pair. A workshop cut whatever thread its own lathe produced, and a bolt taken from one machine would not enter the nut of another. Joseph Whitworth measured samples from many English shops, took an average of the angles and pitches he found, and published the result as a proposal. He had no authority to impose it.

What made the proposal spread was not its merit as engineering — several later systems cut a better thread — but the railway. Rolling stock crossed company boundaries and broke down far from home, and a company that stocked one size of spare could repair a wagon it had not built.

This is the ordinary shape of a standard. Its value to any one adopter rises with the number of others who have adopted it, so the first adopters gain least. A standard that is merely better rarely displaces one that is merely earlier.
prompt: [Academic — Economics] According to the passage, Whitworth arrived at his proposed thread by
choices: improving on a standard published earlier.

correct_answer: taking an average of the angles and pitches already in use.
explanation: He measured samples from many shops and took an average, which is the option about averaging what was in use. Nothing suggests he optimised for strength; the railway spread the standard rather than supplying it; and the passage says a screw and its nut were made as a pair before 1841, so there was no earlier standard to improve.

passage:
The shipping container is often credited to a single design decision. The corner casting — the steel block at each of eight corners, with an oval hole that a twist-lock enters — is what allows a container to be lifted, stacked, and locked to a chassis by the same fitting anywhere in the world. Its dimensions were fixed in a standard published in 1965.

The negotiation that produced them was not technical. Existing fleets used incompatible sizes, and whichever size was chosen, the operators of the others faced the cost of replacement. Agreement was reached only after the United States Maritime Administration made subsidies conditional on compliance, and after the owner of the largest fleet released his own patents royalty-free.

Both moves changed the arithmetic rather than the engineering. What had to be overcome was not the difficulty of agreeing on a shape but the reluctance of those who would lose by the shape chosen.

correct_answer: lifted, stacked, and locked by one fitting anywhere.
explanation: The casting and its twist-lock are introduced precisely as what allows the same fitting to work worldwide. Ship size is never discussed; the point of fixing the dimensions was to remove the several sizes rather than to permit them; and inspection is not mentioned.
